children.translated_text: First Canto
With the sun fierce and the moon longed for,
with water reserves diminished by constant immersion,
delightful in the latter part of the day, with the passion of love subsided,
this summer season has arrived, O beloved.
The nights, with their darkness dispelled by the moon's rays,
houses with wonderful water-fountains here and there,
gem-studded ramparts, and cooling sandalwood paste—
in the hot season, beloved, these become sought after by people.
The fragrant palace terrace, charming,
wine stirred by the breath from a beloved's face,
song accompanied by the lute, kindling desire—
lovers enjoy these in the hot season's beautiful nights.
With their rounded hips clad in fine silk and girdles,
with breasts adorned with pearl necklaces and sandalwood,
with hair perfumed by bathing unguents,
women allay the summer heat of their lovers.
By the feet of voluptuous women, deeply reddened with lac dye,
adorned with anklets,
imitating the call of swans at every step,
the minds of people are filled with desire.
Breasts anointed with sandalwood paste,
adorned with garlands of pearls white as frost,
and hips adorned with golden girdles—
whose mind do they not fill with longing?
With perspiration rising at the joints of their limbs,
casting off their heavy garments now,
upon their breasts, these full-bosomed young women
place only a thin cloth.
By breezes born of fans wet with sandalwood water,
by the placing of pearl necklaces upon the circles of their breasts,
by the sweet sounds of the <s>vallakī</s> (lute) and <s>kākalī</s> (a musical mode)—
<s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love) is awakened today, as if from sleep.
Upon white palaces at night, the faces of women
sleeping in pleasure—the moon
having gazed upon them, surely becomes greatly agitated, and for long,
at the end of night, turns pale as if from shame.
With swirling dust clouds raised by unbearable wind,
the earth scorched by the fierce sun's heat
cannot even be looked upon by travelers
whose hearts are already burnt by the fire of separation from their beloveds.
Deer, greatly tormented by the fierce sun's heat,
their palates parched with intense thirst,
rush through the forest toward water,
having seen the sky dark as split collyrium.
With playful, smiling, sidelong glances,
graceful women, in the minds of travelers,
quickly kindle the fire of <s>Anaṅga</s> (the bodiless god of love),
just as the early evenings adorned with the beautiful moon do.
Greatly scorched by the rays of the sun,
burning on the path with heated dust,
with face cast down, moving crookedly, panting repeatedly,
a serpent sits beneath the shade of a peacock's tail.
Its vigor and effort destroyed by great thirst,
panting repeatedly with jaws widely stretched,
the lion does not strike the elephants even when close by,
its tongue lolling, the tips of its mane trembling.
With water droplets rising from their dried-up throats,
tormented by the rays of the sun,
afflicted by intense thirst, seeking water,
the elephants do not even fear the lions.
By the sun's rays like sacrificial fire,
peacocks, weary in body and spirit,
do not strike the serpent dwelling nearby,
its face nestled within the circles of their tail-feathers.
Digging in the lake with dried mud and <s>bhadramustā</s> (a type of grass),
with long rows of snouts,
greatly scorched by the rays of the sun,
a herd of boars seems to burrow into the earth.
Scorched by the sun with its exceedingly sharp garland of rays,
from the lake with its muddy water,
a frog leaps out and sits
beneath the umbrella-like hood of a thirsty serpent.
With all the networks of lotus stalks pulled up,
its fish perished, its <s>sārasa</s> (cranes) fled in haste,
by elephants pressing together upon one another,
the lake is made thick with churned-up mud.
Its crest-gem's luster broken by the sun's radiance,
the wind licked by its two flickering tongues,
tormented by the heat of its own venom, fire, and the sun, the serpent,
overcome by thirst, does not strike the frog colony.
With mouths covered in foamy saliva,
with blood-red tongues protruding, faces upturned,
overcome by thirst, emerging from mountain caves,
a herd of buffalo gazes toward water.
With sprouting grasses withered by the exceedingly fierce heat of the wildfire,
with dried leaves scattered by the force of harsh winds,
with water diminished all around by the sun's heat,
the forest regions, when beheld, inspire great fear.
Flocks of birds pant upon trees with fallen leaves,
troops of monkeys, exhausted, seek the mountain groves,
herds of <s>gavaya</s> (wild oxen) wander everywhere seeking water,
and the <s>śarabha</s> (a mythical eight-legged beast) draws water straight up from wells.
With a blaze bright as blossoming <s>kusumbha</s> (safflower) and clear vermilion,
swiftly intensified by the force of powerful winds,
entangling the creepers and treetops along the banks,
the wildfire has burnt the earth in every direction.
Intensified by wind, it blazes in the caverns of mountains,
it crackles with sharp sounds in the dry bamboo groves,
it spreads through the grass, gaining strength in an instant,
the forest fire, clinging to the edges, torments the herds of deer.
Seeming to multiply in the forests of <s>śālmalī</s> (silk-cotton trees),
blazing gold-bright in the hollows of trees,
leaping up to tall trees with their branches of withered leaves,
the fire, driven by wind, roams everywhere through the forest.
Elephants, wild oxen, and lions, their bodies scorched by fire,
come together like friends, abandoning their natural enmity;
swiftly emerging from the thicket, distressed by the wildfire,
they enter the broad sandy banks of the river.
With waters filled with lotus groves, delightful with pink depths,
with pleasant sprinklings of cool water, with moonbeams and garlands to enjoy,
may your summer, O beloved, pass in the company of beautiful women,
on the palace rooftop at night, with sweet songs and comfort.
Second Canto
With clouds like rutting elephants bearing fine spray,
with lightning for its banners and thunder for its drums,
the rainy season has arrived like a king, resplendent in its glory,
dear to those who love, O beloved.
With clouds having the hue of deep blue lotus petals,
some resembling heaps of freshly split collyrium,
some having the luster of the breasts of women heavy with child,
the sky is covered with clouds on all sides.
Implored by flocks of thirsty <s>cātaka</s> (rain-birds),
hanging heavy with their burden of water,
the rain clouds move slowly, pouring rain in many streams,
their sound pleasing to the ear and mind.
The rain clouds, with thunder for their drums,
bearing <s>Indra</s>'s bow (the rainbow) strung with lightning,
with their fierce arrows of sharp, falling rain-drops,
strike forcefully at the hearts of travelers.
Covered with grass shoots resembling split emeralds,
spread with the risen leaves of <s>kandalī</s> (plantain),
adorned with gems other than white—
the earth shines like a beautiful woman, with <s>indragopaka</s> (scarlet insects) as her jewels.
Always delightful, eager for the festival of their cries,
adorned with their widely spread, splendid tail-feathers,
agitated by the frenzy of embracing and kissing,
the flock of peacocks has begun its dance today.
Toppling the trees along their banks on all sides,
with swollen, turbid waters of great force,
like thoroughly wicked women who have lost all sense of propriety,
the rivers rush swiftly toward the ocean.
With tufts of grass sprouting tender shoots,
dotted with dark ones nibbled by the mouths of does,
the <s>Vindhya</s> forests captivate the mind,
adorned by trees putting forth new leaves.
With deer all around, their beautiful faces adorned by restless lotus-petal eyes,
newly startled,
the sandy woodland
stirs longing in the heart.
Even in nights made pitch dark
by the clouds thundering loudly and incessantly,
with lightning flashes revealing the path before them,
women go forth to meet their lovers, driven by passion.
By clouds with deep, terrifying rumbles,
and by lightning that greatly agitates their hearts,
women embrace their lovers on the bed without pause,
even those against whom they had borne a grievance.
With tears like drops of water from lotus-like eyes,
upon their beautiful <s>bimba</s>-fruit-red lower lips,
having cast off garlands, ornaments, and unguents,
the wives of travelers stand bereft of hope.
Pale, carrying bits of insects, grass,
creeping in winding paths like a serpent,
watched with alarm by the frog colonies,
the fresh water flows toward the lowlands.
Leaving eagerly the lotus pond now bereft of leaves and flowers,
bees with their sounds pleasing to the ear
fall, deluded, upon the tail-fan circles
of the dancing peacocks, mistaking them for fresh blue lotuses.
Of forest elephants, trumpeting again and again
in excitement at the sound of fresh rain clouds,
the temples, lustrous as spotless blue lotuses,
are covered with swarms of bees drawn to their ichor.
With rocks kissed by clouds bright as white lotuses,
surrounded on all sides by waterfalls,
teeming with peacocks that have begun their dance,
the mountains inspire a feeling of longing.
Shaking the groves of <s>kadamba</s>, <s>sarja</s>, <s>arjuna</s>, and <s>ketakī</s>,
fragrant with their blossoms,
cooled by contact with clouds bearing fine spray,
the breeze—whom does it not fill with longing?
With tresses hanging down to the slopes of their hips,
with fragrant flowers worn as ear-ornaments,

children.text: protkaṇṭhayanti na mano bhuvi kasya yūnaḥ
pradiśatu himayuktaḥ kāla eṣaḥ sukhaṃ vaḥ

children.translated_text: languid with intoxication and infused with musk (<s>mṛganābhi</s>).
Swiftly discarding heavy garments,
people don thin ones dyed with lac (<s>lākṣā</s>) resin,
perfumed with fragrant dark aloe-wood (<s>kālāguru</s>) incense,
[their] limbs languid with the intoxication of desire (<s>kāma</s>).
The male cuckoo (<s>puṃskokila</s>), intoxicated by the wine of mango sap,
kisses his beloved, thrilled with passion;
the bee, buzzing, resting upon a lotus,
makes sweet flattery to his beloved.
The mango trees, bowed down with clusters of copper-red new shoots,
their beautiful branches in bloom,
shaken by the wind, make
the minds of women restless with desire.
Copper-red from the root like coral,
bearing masses of flowers along with their shoots,
the <s>aśoka</s> trees make the hearts of those in the bloom of youth sorrowful,
when gazed upon by them.
With beautiful flowers kissed by intoxicated bees,
with soft new shoots bending in the gentle breeze,
the creepers newly released by the <s>bālā</s> [trees], when beheld,
suddenly arouse eagerness in the hearts of lovers.
Of the <s>kurabaka</s> flower-clusters that have recently appeared,
possessing the radiance of beloved women's faces — their supreme beauty —
having seen [them], what sensitive person's heart would not be
tormented by the falling of <s>Kandarpa</s>'s (the god of love's) arrows?
With <s>kiṃśuka</s> (flame-of-the-forest) groves everywhere, bowed with blossoms,
shaken by winds [and glowing] like blazing fire,
this earth, instantly adorned by the spring season,
shines like a new bride wearing a red garment.
Has it not already been pierced by <s>kiṃśuka</s> flowers, bright as a parrot's beak?
Has it not already been burned by <s>karṇikāra</s> blossoms?
Yet this cuckoo, with his sweet calls,
again strikes the hearts of young men already fixed upon beautiful-faced women.
By male cuckoos with melodious voices, seized with delight,
by buzzing bees uttering intoxicated notes,
the hearts of young brides — bashful and modest — are in an instant
made agitated, even in [their] family homes.
Shaking the flowering branches of mango trees,
spreading the cuckoo's song in all directions,
the wind blows, stealing the hearts of men,
delightful in spring, with the departure of the fall of frost.
With <s>kunda</s> (jasmine) flowers — white as the laughter of a playful bride —
the illuminated pleasure-gardens are enchanting;
they steal the heart even of a sage free from passion,
how much more the minds of young men, stained with desire!
With trailing golden girdles, necklaces clinging to their breasts,
their bodily grace made languid by the pride of <s>Kandarpa</s> (Cupid),
in the month of <s>Madhu</s> (spring), with the sounds of sweet cuckoos and bees,
women forcibly steal the hearts of men.
Adorned with trees bearing various delightful blossoms,
their mountain-slopes resounding with the joyful cries of various birds,
their rock-surfaces wound about with networks of mountain-herbs,
seeing the mountains, all people are filled with delight.
He closes his eyes, he weeps, he is overcome with sorrow,
he blocks his nose with his hand, he cries out aloud —
the traveler, his mind afflicted by separation from his beloved,
upon seeing the flowering mango trees.
With the calls of intoxicated bees and cuckoos,
with flowering mangoes and <s>karṇikāra</s> trees, [the month is] lovely;
like sharp arrows, it pierces the minds of proud women,
the flower-month (<s>kusumamāsa</s>), for the kindling of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love).
The flowering mango trees, releasing heaps of blossoms
with the splendor of beautiful gold, shaken by a gentle wind —
gazing directly upon them, even the emaciated traveler on the road
falls into a swoon from the blows of <s>Madana</s>'s (Cupid's) arrows.
With the cuckoo's delightful, melodious songs [mocking] sweet speech,
with the radiance of <s>kunda</s> (jasmine) blossoms [mocking] the rays of smiling teeth,
with sprouts red as coral [mocking] the beauty of tender hand-shoots,
spring now mocks the women of desire.
With faces [glowing] like golden lotuses, cheeks pale [with longing],
with necklaces resting above [their breasts], breast-tips moist with sandal-paste,
with glances full of coquetry born of intoxication, women
desire even the greatest sages, bowed by the weight of their breasts, [those sages being] tranquil.
The face-lotus is fragrant with spring-honey, the eyes are copper-red like <s>lodhra</s> [blossoms],
the mass of hair, filled with fresh <s>kurabaka</s> flowers, is charming,
the pair of breasts is heavy, the hips [are round] as well —
what of women's [charms] is not now an instrument of <s>Manmatha</s> (the god of love)?
The hearts of proud women are shaken
by winds perfumed by full-blown mango blossoms,
by the calls of the intoxicated cuckoo,
and by the pleasing song-sounds of the bee.
The evening hour, lovely with the bright moon's radiance,
the call of the male cuckoo, the fragrant wind,
the buzzing of swarms of intoxicated bees, the drinking of wine at night —
all this is an elixir for the Flower-weaponed One (<s>Kusumāyudha</s>, i.e., <s>Kāma</s>).
With lips fashioned like red <s>aśoka</s> [blossoms], sweet — [his] voice the sound of intoxicated bees,
with a row of teeth pure-white as a <s>kunda</s>-flower garland, with a face [radiant] as a fully-bloomed lotus,
with a breeze gentle and fragrant with the scent of mango blossoms — the preceptor in the initiation of <s>śṛṅgāra</s> (erotic sentiment) —

children.text: kalpāntaṃ madanapriyo diśatu vaḥ puṣpāgamo maṅgalam
children.translated_text: may the arrival of flowers (<s>puṣpāgama</s>), dear to <s>Madana</s> (Cupid), bestow auspiciousness upon you until the end of the <s>kalpa</s> (cosmic age)!
Pierced by the <s>Malaya</s> mountain breeze, delightful with the cuckoo's song,
having obtained a continuous stream of fragrance from the showering of sweet nectar,
surrounded on all sides by swarms of diverse bees —
may spring, the most excellent of seasons, bring you happiness!
The mango blossom-cluster is his lovely arrow, the beautiful <s>kiṃśuka</s> is his bow,

children.text: jyā yasyālikulaṃ kalaṅkarahitaṃ chattraṃ sitāṃśuḥ sitam
children.translated_text: the string of bees is his bowstring, the spotless white moon is his white parasol,
the intoxicated elephant is the <s>Malaya</s> wind, the cuckoo is his herald — the conqueror of the world!
May that <s>Manmatha</s> (Cupid), accompanied by spring, abundantly bestow blessings upon you!
